ingredients.name: Ash plantains (raw, unripe)
ingredients.notes: about 500g after peeling; green/raw plantains can substitute if ash plantains unavailable. Have a bowl of turmeric-salted water ready to submerge pieces immediately after cutting to prevent browning.

ingredients.name: Turmeric powder
ingredients.notes: split: 1/4 tsp for soaking water, 1/4 tsp for the curry

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.notes: 1 cup, for cooking the plantain before adding coconut milk

steps.instruction: Prepare a bowl of cold water with 1/4 tsp turmeric and a pinch of salt. Peel the ash plantains, removing all traces of the green outer skin, and cut diagonally into 2-3cm pieces, dropping each piece immediately into the turmeric-salt water to prevent browning.

Drain the plantain pieces. Add them directly to a cooking pot along with the onion, curry leaves, pandan leaf, cinnamon stick, mustard seeds, fenugreek (if using), green chillies, remaining turmeric, and salt.

Pour in the water. Bring to a boil over medium heat, then cover and simmer for about 15 minutes, until the plantain pieces are just tender when pierced with a fork -- they should be cooked through but still hold their shape.

Pour in the thick coconut milk. Stir gently and simmer uncovered over low heat for 5-8 minutes, until the gravy thickens slightly and the plantain is fully cooked. Avoid boiling vigorously after adding coconut milk.
Taste and adjust salt. Serve hot with rice. This is considered a mild 'white curry' (kiri hodi style) so it pairs well alongside spicier dishes.

source_site: islandsmile.org, cross-checked against kitchensimmer.com, joyofeatingtheworld.com, theceylonchef.co.uk, theperfectcurry.com, and infolanka.com
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 6+ independent sources; universal agreement on immediate submersion in turmeric-salt water and the mild white-curry approach
notes: Ash plantain (alu kesel) is a starchy, mildly-flavoured variety of plantain used specifically for cooking savoury dishes in Sri Lanka -- it is never eaten ripe. The immediate submersion in turmeric-salt water after peeling is critical: ash plantain oxidises and browns within seconds of air exposure. The mild, creamy result suits even those who generally avoid spicy food, making it a popular choice for children and elderly family members. A fried variant (badapu alu kesel curry) -- where the slices are first shallow-fried before adding to the gravy -- is also common and forms part of the lamprais set (sl_045). Green plantains widely available outside Sri Lanka are the most reliable substitute.
